## Model selection

**Default to Sonnet 5 (what you're on now) for most of the CLI_PLAN milestones.** Once a milestone has a clear spec and definition of done — which M1, M2, M4, M6, M8, M10, M12–M14 all do — that's mechanical-enough work that Sonnet at high effort is both sufficient and meaningfully cheaper/faster than Opus. Don't pay Opus prices for "implement the Zod schema from the doc."

**Reserve Opus 4.8 for the genuinely hard, high-blast-radius pieces:**
- **M3, the identity resolver.** Our own docs call it "the hardest and most important part" — it has the most interacting edge cases (amend/rebase/squash/split/cherry-pick/filter-repo) and getting it subtly wrong corrupts data silently rather than throwing an error. This is worth an Opus first-pass design, not just an Opus review.
- **M7's redaction pass and M9's embedding/vector-store wiring** if either starts feeling fiddly — redaction is security-relevant (a wrong regex leaks a secret into a synced git object), and the transformers.js/sqlite-vec integration is the other place with real "did this actually work" uncertainty rather than pure typing.
- **A dedicated review pass**, even on Sonnet-written code, for M3 and M7 specifically — you have `/code-review` at `high`/`xhigh` effort available, and pointing that at just those two milestones once written is a good use of Opus without re-running it on the boilerplate.

**Concrete switch trigger, rather than a vibe:** if Sonnet's first attempt at something produces logic that's subtly wrong twice in a row, or you notice yourself re-explaining an edge case a third time, that's the signal to stop iterating on Sonnet and hand the same problem to Opus fresh — don't let a stuck Sonnet loop burn more turns than a clean Opus attempt would've cost.

**Fable 5, honestly:** I don't have reliable first-hand knowledge of what it's specifically good at relative to Sonnet/Opus — it's newer to me than the other two. Since it's gone in 2 days, the highest-value use of that window is a cheap empirical test rather than trusting my guess: run **M1 (easy, schemas)** and **M3 (hard, identity resolver)** through it once each and compare against what Sonnet/Opus produce. That gives you a real data point on where it sits before the option disappears, instead of speculation from me.

## Keeping implementation context separate from planning context

The core problem: this conversation now carries the full research debate, rejected framings, and every intermediate decision. None of that belongs in a session that's just implementing M1. The fix isn't a tool setting, it's a discipline:

1. **The docs are the interface, not the conversation.** `CLI_PLAN.md`, `DATA_MODEL.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md` exist specifically so a cold-start session never needs this conversation's history — that's why they have explicit "Assumptions and judgment calls" sections instead of leaving reasoning implicit. If a fresh session ever needs to ask "wait, why did we choose X" that a doc should already answer, that's a doc gap to fix, not a reason to drag conversation history along.

2. **Start a new session per milestone (or small group of milestones), not a continuation of this one.** Point it at exactly what it needs — e.g. "Implement Milestone 1 from `architecture/CLI_PLAN.md`; read that section plus `DATA_MODEL.md` §1–5, nothing else." That's a small, cheap, focused context instead of replaying a multi-hour planning session.

3. **For work that's well-specified and low-interaction, delegate to a subagent instead of a new top-level session** — same mechanism I used for the research fan-out. A subagent starts cold by design, so it structurally can't inherit this conversation's bloat; it only gets what's in your prompt plus what it reads from disk. This suits milestones like M1, M2, M4 well. It suits M3 less well if you want to interactively steer the trickiest logic — for that, a fresh interactive session (possibly on Opus, per above) beats a fire-and-forget subagent.

4. **Use worktree isolation for anything you'd run in parallel.** The `Agent` tool's `isolation: "worktree"` option gives each milestone its own working copy of the repo, so two milestones being built at once can't collide on files, on top of not colliding on conversation context.

5. **Don't keep "planning mode" and "implementation mode" in the same thread going forward.** Now that the plan docs exist, treat this conversation as closed for planning purposes. New implementation work should open fresh, cite the doc + milestone number, and stop there — resist the pull to say "continue from where we left off" in a chat that still remembers every idea we rejected along the way.

The practical test for whether a doc is "complete enough" to be the boundary: could a new session implement the milestone correctly having read *only* the cited doc sections, with zero conversation history? Right now I'd say yes for M1/M2/M4 and most of the CLI-wiring milestones; M3 is the one place I'd actually want a human (you) in the loop live rather than trusting a cold-start session to get every edge case right unsupervised.

body.text:
Everything checks out on the testbed. Here's the full audit against your "original git stuff won't vanish" concern:

**What was tested and proven:**
1. **Hooks can never break a commit** — I made a normal commit with the hooks installed and `git-for-ai` deliberately *not* on PATH. Git printed `command not found`, the `|| true` swallowed it, and the commit succeeded. Worst-case failure mode is a noisy warning, never a blocked or corrupted commit.
2. **All 11 original commit SHAs are byte-identical** — the ledger attaches via git notes, which never touch the commit objects. `git log` before and after: same SHAs, same graph.
3. **Exactly two new refs were created**, both in their own namespaces: `refs/notes/git-for-ai/intent` and `refs/git-for-ai/change-map`. `refs/heads/main` was never touched.
4. **`git fsck` is clean** — no dangling or corrupt objects.
5. **The intent data is plain, inspectable JSON** living in ordinary git storage (I dumped a raw note above — human-readable envelope, exactly matching the spec). Complete removal is two commands: `git update-ref -d refs/notes/git-for-ai/intent` and `git update-ref -d refs/git-for-ai/change-map`, plus deleting `.git-for-ai/` — the repo returns to exactly its pre-init state.

**And the payoff works**: after seeding two commits with real ledger entries (simulating what the M7 capture hook will do automatically), `log --intent` renders real intent lines — summaries, confidence, agent attribution — side by side with honest `[no intent: pre-git-for-ai]` rows for unseeded history.

Two known rough edges, both already on the radar: the `command not found` hook noise disappears once the CLI is npm-linked onto PATH (or we add stderr suppression to the hook script), and new commits don't get Change-Id trailers yet because the `internal-hook` dispatch command is a later milestone.

Given this evidence I'd say initializing the `git-for-ai` repo itself is safe whenever you want — say the word and I'll dogfood it. Meanwhile M7 (session capture) and M8 (`show`) are still building in the background; when they land, the real test is a live Claude Code session against the testbed with automatic capture.

Almost — they're not modifying git's own commands at all. `git-for-ai` is a standalone binary, and git has a built-in convention where `git for-ai <cmd>` automatically finds any `git-<name>` executable on PATH and runs it as if it were a subcommand (same trick `git lfs` and `git flow` use).

So `git for-ai log --intent`, `git for-ai blame --why`, etc. are *parallel* commands that read your repo plus the extra intent refs — your normal `git log`, `git blame`, and everything else remain completely untouched.

Yes — for decades, and at several layers, which is exactly what this project leans on:

- **Subcommands** (~2006-era behavior): any executable named `git-<something>` on PATH becomes `git something`. That's the whole install story for `git lfs`, `git flow`, and us.
- **Hooks** (since the very early days): scripts git runs at lifecycle points (`commit-msg`, `post-commit`, `post-rewrite`...) — how we observe commits and rewrites.
- **Refs and notes as open namespaces**: anything can store data under its own `refs/*` without touching branches — how Gerrit, git-lfs, git-annex, and our intent ledger all coexist inside a plain repo.

The design bet of this project is basically that git's extension points are rich enough that "AI-augmented source control" needs zero forking — and so far every milestone has confirmed it.
